claims.text: As-synthesized multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles have homogeneous bulk compositions with minimal surface segregation.
High-temperature structural and chemical stability is governed by the interplay between configurational entropy and controlled surface segregation.
Modest enrichment of selected surface elements forms a passivating layer.
The proposed passivating surface layer suppresses further atomic or surface diffusion.
Suppressing diffusion through surface passivation prevents deleterious surface phase separation and preserves a compositionally homogeneous core.
High configurational entropy in near-equiatomic nanoparticles retards bulk atomic diffusion.
High configurational entropy retards phase coarsening.
Nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloys can exhibit high thermal stability and no detectable grain growth under extreme-environment testing.
Refractory high-entropy alloys are candidates for elevated-temperature applications because of their resistance to softening and high melting points.
The proposed nanoparticles are applicable across catalytic temperatures of 773–1173 K and thermoelectric temperatures of 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticles engineered to favor slight surface segregation will coarsen more slowly than uniformly composed nanoparticles under identical high-temperature exposure.
Nanoparticles engineered to favor slight surface segregation will undergo less phase separation than uniformly composed nanoparticles.
The segregation-engineered nanoparticles will retain a more stable morphology and show slower grain-boundary evolution.
The segregation-engineered nanoparticles will maintain overall compositional homogeneity in their cores.
A strictly homogeneous baseline with no induced surface segregation is more susceptible to diffusion-driven phase separation and coarsening.
The proposed mechanism is limited to particles below a critical size at which diffusion lengths are comparable to particle size.
Strong support interactions or oxidative environments may override or alter the proposed entropy-and-segregation mechanism.

Failure of the segregation-engineered particles to form a passivating layer or to show a statistically significant reduction in coarsening or phase separation relative to the uniform control would falsify the hypothesis.
